entry.title: [推荐] Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Jessica Croteau

Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. entry.title: [推荐] The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Caio Simoneti

This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. entry.title: [推荐] Difference‐Making Under Metaphysical Indeterminacy
entry.content:
Philosophy & Public Affairs · Vol. 54 No. 4 262-273 · 推荐 (4.0)

Jessica Li

Many of the most pressing moral problems we face involve collective harms generated by large numbers of individually insignificant actions. Unlike triggering cases—where a threshold exists such that a single act could be decisive—non‐triggering cases lack any such sharp cutoff. In these cases, no individual act appears to make a difference to whether harm occurs, and it may be metaphysically indeterminate whether a given aggregate is harmful or whether a marginal contribution plays any causal role at all. I argue that standard approaches to moral responsibility, which rely on difference‐making or expected outcomes, struggle to provide action‐guiding reasons in these contexts. entry.title: [推荐] Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (3.0)

Karolin I. M. Tuncel、Tobias Müller

Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. Rita Koganzon

Political theorists have long focused their understanding of democratic education on the institution of the school, particularly the public school, to the exclusion of broader visions of education beyond schooling. But as criticisms of schooling from outside the academy mount, it becomes imperative to examine the origins of American educational thought to determine whether opposition to schooling has an older historical source. This essay locates the roots of school skepticism in an alternative American educational tradition beginning with Benjamin Franklin that drew on Locke’s pedagogical arguments to devalue institutional schooling in favor of self-education. This interview with the philosopher Raymond Geuss, Professor Emeritus of Philosophy at the University of Cambridge, explores the questions animating his 2026 book Tracks in Chaos: Philosophical Orientation and Political Reflection (Polity). entry.title: [推荐] The Utilitarian Classical Liberalism of Ludwig von Mises and Its Libertarian Misreception
entry.content:
Political Theory · Vol. 54 No. 5 749-772 · 推荐 (3.0)

Jonathan Cole

This article examines Ludwig von Mises’s utilitarianism in the context of his liberal social theory. It contends that he sought to reorient classical liberalism away from natural law theory and refound it in utilitarianism. This significant shift distinguishes and differentiates Misesian liberalism from the classical liberal tradition with which Mises consciously identified it, as well as later Rothbardian libertarianism, which, while identifying with the Misesian tradition, reverted to a natural law philosophy that produced irreconcilable differences with Misesian liberalism over the legitimacy of the state.

Nicholas A. Anderson

The fact that Toward Perpetual Peace is presented as a satirical peace treaty is a detail that has been largely overlooked in the literature. This article argues that when one reads Toward Perpetual Peace with its formal presentation in mind, what emerges is a work of philosophical literature that acts politically through its rhetorical form. The article shows how Kant—through what is here called his rhetoric of hope—offers a political education to two kinds of readers: the many, who are susceptible to a “despotic” moralism, and the elite, who embrace the principles of a selfish despotism. This article offers a feminist reworking of Adriana Cavarero’s conceptualization of horrorism as a form of extreme violence that targets and dehumanizes its victims through dismemberment and an ontological assault on human uniqueness. The binary risks reproducing the very logics of exclusion and moral absolutism it seeks to disrupt. entry.content:
Political Theory · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.0)

Ross Carroll

Edmund Burke’s thoughts on plantation slavery have long been the subject of scholarly attention. Too often, however, discerning Burke’s long-term intention in relation to slavery has taken precedence over examining the specific administrative strategies he proposed for managing enslaved populations in the interim. Seeking to remedy this gap, the article reads Burke’s Sketch for a Negro Code as an exercise in colonial ameliorationism; that is, a reform programme that looked to ameliorate the institution of slavery as a way of strengthening British colonialism in the West Indies and civilising the African coast. entry.title: [推荐] "A Place Dedicated to Openness of Mind": Why Academic Freedom Protects "Distasteful" Extramural Speech
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 682-706 · 推荐 (3.0)

Nicholas Tampio

: This article explains why academic freedom protects "distasteful" extramural speech, including social media posts outside of a scholar's area of expertise. Initially, I explain why using the First Amendment to protect academic freedom jeopardizes the latter. Next, I describe how German philosophers and American pragmatists expounded academic freedom to protect a community of strong-willed scholars. Then, I note that the AAUP has backed away from defending the Enlightenment-Romantic conception of the good supporting academic freedom. Finally, I argue that academic freedom should protect both Plato and Diogenes, polite and confrontational scholars.

entry.title: [推荐] Portraits of Absence: Listening to the Kidnapped Posters
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 707-740 · 推荐 (3.0)

Alyson Cole

: Images are sites and key media of struggle. This essay shows how such conflicts play out—both via form and through use—and why that matters for the study of politics. Analyzing the visual politics of #KidnappedFromIsrael provides a critical yet undertheorized perspective on the hostilities that erupted in American cities over Israel/Palestine after October 7. Through this case study I endeavor to make four contributions: 1. define a visual genre, "portraits of absence," which publicizes suffering in distinct ways; 2. extend critical phenomenologists' conceptualization of "perceptual habits" to the not-Other; 3. explicate and trouble binaries undergirding empathic visual practices; 4. reassess the relationship between virtual and physical sites of political contestation.

: This article investigates the role of trafficking narratives in early-twentieth-century liberal internationalist world-making. Focusing on the League of Nations' anti-trafficking campaign, I demonstrate how these efforts contributed to such liberal worldmaking through what I call under worldmaking. I use Edward Said's notion of imaginative geography to explore the League's fixation with the relationship between global civility and global criminality, treating it as an adaptation of imperialism's Manichaean geopolitics for the new internationalist age. I focus on the Traffic in Women and Children's committee's process of knowledge production, arguing that the parallel trafficking underworld they worked so hard to capture also shared figurative entailments with antisemitic conspiracy theories. entry.title: [推荐] The Collapse of Shame: Corruption as Genre in a Post-Truth Age. Toward a Cultural Theory of Public Impunity
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 775-786 · 推荐 (3.0)

Jacqueline Fendt

: This essay argues that corruption today functions not as scandal but as genre—performed, aestheticized, and infrastructurally sustained. In an era where shame collapses and impropriety becomes spectacle, corruption no longer hides: it signals power. Impunity now takes shape as public demonstration, staged and circulated as proof of sovereignty. Corruption, shame, and impunity form a new circuitry: corruption provides the recognizable form, shame recedes into spectacle, and impunity choreographs authority through performance. To understand democratic erosion today, we must analyze and expose this choreography—not only legally, but culturally, emotionally, and structurally.

entry.title: [推荐] Complaints about the Weather: Eco-Neurosis in Jonathan Safran Foer and Jenny Offill
entry.content:
Theory & Event · Vol. 29 No. 4 787-813 · 推荐 (3.0)

Hans Demeyer

: This essay identifies eco-neurosis as an affective response to the environmental crisis. Aware that their lives contribute to this crisis, the eco-neurotic polices their consumption and lifestyle patterns, yet simultaneously remains attached to the good life promise under capitalism: a double bind that causes compulsive thoughts and feelings. If such eco-neurosis causes an affective displacement, this essay proposes the complaint as a genre that expresses such neurosis and offers the promise of renewed belonging. A reading of eco-neurosis in Jonathan Safran Foer's We Are the Weather (2019) and Jenny Offill's Weather (2020) shows how the complaint however preserves the double bind.
